statement: Diné sandpainting is intentionally ephemeral — destroyed at the close of each healing ceremony — and traditional restriction against outsider observation and permanent reproduction is real and documented. Nancy J. Parezo, Navajo Sandpainting: From Religious Act to Commercial Art (University of Arizona Press, 1983), documents the 20th-century commercialization of sandpainting imagery into a secular/tourist art form (including woven-rug reproductions) as a genuine, citable controversy — a shift "from a sacred to a secular domain and from native use to non-native consumption." Per this project's ethical constraint, this claim reports the existence and general structure of the restriction and its commercialization history; no ceremonial sandpainting content is described or reconstructed.

sources.citation: Parezo, Nancy J. Navajo Sandpainting: From Religious Act to Commercial Art. Tucson: University of Arizona Press, 1983.
sources.author: Nancy J. Parezo
